title: Algorithmic approach to adiabatic quantum optimization
abstract_summary: The paper proposes a simple iterative adiabatic quantum optimization algorithm that mitigates exponentially small gaps caused by perturbative anticrossings between eigenstates associated with local and global minima. By rapidly sampling local minima after non-adiabatic passes and adjusting single-qubit tunneling amplitudes to penalize pathways to those minima, the method is shown via quantum Monte Carlo simulations to solve hard 64-qubit maximum independent set instances with many degenerate local minima in on the order of ten iterations.
methodology_description: The authors study perturbative anticrossings that produce exponentially small gaps in adiabatic quantum optimization (AQO) and introduce a heuristic, iterative algorithm that adaptively modifies single-qubit transverse (tunnelling) energies (∆i) to penalize paths to clusters of degenerate local minima. They generate hard test instances of the Maximum Independent Set (MIS) problem (64-node graphs with a unique MIS) by a targeted graph-construction procedure that creates many highly-degenerate maximal independent sets clustered by 2‑bit flips. Simulations are performed with path-integral Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) using A(s) and B(s) energy schedules taken from superconducting flux-qubit devices; each iteration runs r=500 short (non-adiabatic) anneals (tf = 0.08 µs) to sample local minima reached after anticrossings. From sampled minima they compute per-qubit penalty scores µi (estimated from sampled local minima and single-bit-flip energy costs), and update ∆i using a geometric-update rule ∆i,new ∝ ∆i,old^(1−β) µi^(−β) with β = 1/(κ+1) (κ = iteration index), constraining ∆i to a feasible range [0.25, 8]. Stopping criteria are either an estimated adiabatic time ta < 16 µs (computed via QMC) or that the probability mass in the basin of the global minimum just before a perturbative crossing exceeds 0.005 (so global minimum would be found with high probability in r runs). They report empirical performance over an ensemble of generated 64-node instances and monitor expectation values ⟨σ_z⟩(s) and gap/adiabatic time estimates to confirm elimination of perturbative crossings over iterations.
algorithms_used: Iterative heuristic single-qubit tunnelling adaptation (∆i tuning)
Gradient descent from sampled bitstrings (classical postprocessing)
experimental_setup: Simulations used path-integral Quantum Monte Carlo to emulate quantum annealing with device-like energy schedules A(s) and B(s) (taken from superconducting flux-qubit designs). Each algorithm iteration performed r = 500 anneals of duration tf = 0.08 µs. Problem size: 64 qubits (graphs with 64 nodes, target MIS size 20). ∆i constrained to [0.25, 8]. Sampling and QMC runs were performed on distributed classical resources (AQUA@home volunteers).
experiment_input: Synthetic graph instances for Maximum Independent Set: 64-node graphs, initially 220 randomly selected edges, subsequently modified via a targeted procedure to enforce a unique MIS of size 20 and to create many maximal independent sets clustered by 2-bit flips. Generation algorithm: (1) create 64-node graph with 220 random edges; (2) find an independent set of size 20 to be the MIS; (3) add edges from non-MIS nodes to MIS nodes to make MIS maximal; (4–6) iterate depth-first search to find other independent sets of size 20, modify edges to produce many adjacent maximal independent sets, repeat until no more independent sets of size 20 are found. Of 51 generated graphs, 50 were used as test instances (all exhibiting perturbative anticrossings).
experiment_process: 1) Initialize all ∆i = 1. 2) On each iteration κ: perform r = 500 short anneals (tf = 0.08 µs) via QMC to sample measurement bitstrings. 3) Map sampled bitstrings by classical gradient descent to local maxima/minima to identify maximal independent sets reached; compute per-qubit energies Bk,i for single-qubit flips from sampled minima. 4) Compute µi for each qubit as the sample-average proxy for the curvature contribution (per Eq. (10) in the paper). 5) Update ∆i via ∆i,new = ∆i,old^(1−β) * µi^(−β) with β = 1/(κ+1); rescale ∆i to be within [0.25, 8]. 6) Recompute adiabatic time ta (via QMC-based gap/transition estimates) and/or probability mass in the global-minimum basin; if ta < 16 µs or basin probability > 0.005, stop. 7) Otherwise increment κ and repeat. Iterations continued until success (empirically ≤ 13 iterations; mean ≈ 3).
experiment_output: Outputs: per-instance number of iterations to 'solve' (eliminate perturbative crossing), QMC-estimated adiabatic times ta, probability mass in the basin of the global minimum before anticrossing, and visualization traces of ground-state expectation values ⟨σ_z⟩(s) across s. Success criteria: ta < 16 µs or basin probability > 0.005 (implying >92% chance to find global minimum across r=500 runs). Empirical results: all 50 hard instances solved within 13 iterations; average 3.0 iterations.

reproducibility_notes: The paper details the graph-generation procedure, the iterative ∆i update rule, success criteria, and the QMC-based sampling approach; however, no public code, exact QMC implementation parameters (e.g., Trotter slices, inverse temperature, QMC update schedule), or raw instance files are provided. Simulations were run on AQUA@home volunteer resources. Reproducing results would require reimplementing the QMC setup and graph generation as described.
key_findings: [supported] Perturbative anticrossings with exponentially small gaps between the ground and first excited states can make adiabatic quantum optimization (AQO) inefficient (background claim supported by prior analytic and numerical studies).

[supported] An iterative, heuristic algorithm that adaptively adjusts single-qubit transverse-field strengths (Δi) based on samples of local minima can eliminate perturbative anticrossings in practice (demonstrated via Quantum Monte Carlo simulations on test instances).

[speculative] Low-order perturbation theory explains how second-order curvature (E^(2)) of clusters of local minima controls the occurrence of perturbative crossings, and indicates that changing Δi can alter these curvatures to avoid crossings.
[supported] The authors generated targeted 64-qubit Maximum Independent Set (MIS) instances with extremely many degenerate local minima (10^5–10^6) and a unique global minimum to stress-test AQO.

[supported] Using QMC simulations of the adiabatic evolution (with anneal schedule parameters taken from flux-qubit experiments), the iterative algorithm solved all 50 hard 64-qubit instances within 13 iterations (average 3.0 iterations).

[supported] Practical implementation details used in simulations: per-iteration sampling r = 500 runs, individual anneal time tf = 0.08 μs, and a success criterion tied to adiabatic time ta < 16 μs (which yields >92% chance of sampling the global minimum in an iteration).

[speculative] The algorithm is heuristic and not proven to guarantee elimination of all perturbative crossings for arbitrary instances; success may depend on instance structure and choice of parameters (β schedule, Δi bounds).

[speculative] The approach suggests that tuning available Hamiltonian degrees of freedom (e.g., Δi) can mitigate a class of small-gap problems in AQO, implying that worst-case small gaps are not inevitably fatal if problem/driver parameters can be adjusted.
results_summary: The paper proposes and evaluates a simple iterative AQO strategy that adaptively penalizes paths to clusters of local minima by tuning single-qubit tunnelling energies (Δi). Analytical perturbation arguments motivate the approach by linking second-order energy curvatures of clustered local minima to perturbative crossings. The authors generate hard 64-qubit MIS instances (with 10^5–10^6 degenerate local minima and unique global minima) and use Quantum Monte Carlo simulations with device-like annealing schedules to emulate runs and sampling. Empirically, the heuristic eliminated perturbative crossings and solved all 50 tested instances within 13 iterations (average 3 iterations), demonstrating practical effectiveness on the constructed benchmark suite. The work is a demonstration in simulation rather than a proof of asymptotic performance or a hardware quantum speedup.
performance_claims: [supported] Generated 64-qubit MIS instances having between 10^5 and 10^6 highly-degenerate local minima.
[supported] All 50 hard 64-qubit instances were solved within 13 iterations of the algorithm, with an average of 3.0 iterations required.

[supported] Using per-iteration sampling of r = 500 anneals with anneal time tf = 0.08 μs, if adiabatic time ta < 16 μs then the probability of finding the global minimum at least once in that iteration exceeds 92%.
[supported] The feasible range for Δi in simulations was restricted to [1/4, 8]; Δi values were rescaled each iteration to remain in that range.
[supported] The heuristic parameter schedule used β = 1/(κ + 1) (κ = iteration number) when updating Δi, which empirically provided robust convergence on the tested instances.
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper demonstrates a heuristic parameter-tuning method that, in QMC simulations, removes perturbative anticrossings on constructed hard instances. It does not claim nor demonstrate a provable or empirical quantum computational advantage (no asymptotic speedup or hardware benchmarks showing superiority over classical algorithms are presented).
limitations: The algorithm is heuristic and not guaranteed to find a crossing-free adiabatic path for all instances (authors state objective was not to create a flawless algorithm).
Evaluation and demonstration are limited to 64-qubit problem instances (all tests used 64-node graphs); scalability to larger qubit counts is not demonstrated. [inferred]

Problem-instance generation method used to produce extremely hard test instances requires time exponential in the number of nodes if the desired MIS size grows linearly, limiting applicability of the test methodology to larger graphs (authors explicitly caution about this).

Simulations rely on Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) rather than real quantum hardware; QMC sampling approximates ground-state distributions but may not faithfully capture real-time dynamics, noise, or open-system effects. [inferred]

The approach specifically targets anticrossings that are perturbative in nature (perturbative crossings caused by clusters of local minima); it may not address non-perturbative small-gap phenomena or other mechanisms causing small gaps. [inferred]

The algorithm assumes the ability to tune single-qubit tunneling energies (∆i) over a usable range; practical hardware constraints on tunability and the chosen feasible range (here 1/4 to 8) may limit real-world implementation. [inferred]

Choice of algorithm hyperparameters (number of samples r = 500, anneal time tf = 0.08 µs, β schedule β = 1/(κ+1), feasible ∆i range) was empirical for these tests; robustness and optimal settings across problem classes and sizes are not established. [inferred]

The method depends on being able to sample the local minima that the system occupies after a nonadiabatic crossing; this requires many quick runs and classical postprocessing (gradient descent) which could be costly for larger systems. [inferred]

There is no theoretical proof provided that eliminating perturbative crossings via ∆i tuning guarantees polynomial-time scaling of adiabatic quantum optimization for large instances; empirical success on 64 qubits does not imply a scaling guarantee. [inferred]

The algorithm may oscillate between penalizing different clusters of local minima; while the β schedule was found empirically robust, convergence is not proven and behaviour in more complex landscapes is uncertain. [inferred]

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — An iterative heuristic that adaptively modifies single-qubit transverse-field strengths (Δi) can eliminate perturbative anticrossings and restore viable adiabatic gaps on hard 64-qubit MIS instances, enabling solution within a small number of iterations (mean ≈ 3, ≤13).

#idea:hybrid-approach — The method is hybrid: short (non-adiabatic) anneal samples are collected (via QMC) and classical postprocessing (gradient descent on sampled bitstrings) plus a classical update rule for Δi guide subsequent anneals.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Experiments use device-like A(s), B(s) schedules from superconducting flux-qubit literature and modest Δi ranges ([0.25,8]), suggesting the heuristic could be implementable on quantum annealers with per-qubit driver control.
#limitation:simulation-only — All results are from path-integral Quantum Monte Carlo emulation on classical distributed resources (AQUA@home); no experiments on physical QPUs are reported.
#limitation:qubit-count — Demonstrations are limited to 64-qubit synthetic MIS instances; scalability to larger, practical problem sizes is not shown.
#limitation:no-empirical-validation — Key QMC implementation details (Trotter slices, inverse temperature, update schedules), raw instances and code are not provided, limiting reproducibility.
#limitation:noise — Real-device noise, control errors, and open-system effects are not fully modeled; QMC used device-like schedules but may not capture all hardware error sources.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Success is evidenced by QMC-estimated adiabatic times (ta) falling below a chosen threshold (16 μs) or basin probability exceeding 0.005 after iterative updates, demonstrating practical elimination of targeted anticrossings for the tested ensemble.

#idea:hybrid-approach — The Δi update is a simple geometric rule using sample-derived per-qubit penalty scores μi with iteration-dependent exponent β = 1/(κ+1), bounding Δi to remain within a feasible operational range.
